1.pericope_label: Now when all this was finished, all Israel that were present went out to the cities of Judah, and brake the images in pieces, and cut down the groves, and threw down the high places and the altars out of all Judah and Benjamin, in Ephraim also and Manasseh, until they had utterly destroyed them all. Then all the children of Israel returned, every man to his possession, into their own cities.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the objects broken as standing pillars and the sacred trunks that served as emblems of fertility, renders the closing phrase literally as so far as to finishing, and explains the freedom to act in the north politically: that kingdom was in the last stage of weakness and drifting toward ruin, so the zealots were unlikely to meet serious resistance.
Gill lists what had been finished before the reforming began — the temple cleansed, the ministers sanctified, the passover and the unleavened bread kept, and seven further days of rejoicing.

Clarke declines to decide whether the northern reformation proceeded from a transport of religious zeal or with Hoshea's consent, and surveys the chapter as a sequence ending in a king who prospered because he acted in sincerity and truth; Wesley is definite on both counts, that the people acted by a special impulse of the Spirit and that Hoshea, content with the calves, would suffer the images of Baal to be broken.

Henry makes the sequence the point, that what was wanting in the preparation was made up in the improvement afterwards, and that the comfort of communion with God should kindle an indignation against everything offensive to him; he marks three features of the destruction — that it reached beyond Judah into the northern tribes, that nothing was spared through favour however ancient or costly, and that the people would not go home until it was done.

debates.question: How could the reformers act in Ephraim and Manasseh?

positions.position: Either those cities had passed under Judah, or Hoshea did not forbid it, or the northerners who had come to the passover went home and did it themselves.
It cannot be told whether zeal or royal consent carried them there.
A special impulse of the Spirit, and a king who tolerated it because his own idolatry was the calves rather than Baal.
The northern kingdom was too weak to resist.

themes: Now when all this was finished, all Israel that were present went out to the cities of Judah, and brake the images in pieces, and cut down the groves, and threw down the high places and the altars out of all Judah and Benjamin, in Ephraim also and Manasseh, until they had utterly destroyed them all. Then all the children of Israel returned, every man to his possession, into their own cities.

2.pericope_label: And Hezekiah appointed the courses of the priests and the Levites after their courses, every man according to his service, the priests and Levites for burnt offerings and for peace offerings, to minister, and to give thanks, and to praise in the gates of the tents of the Lord. He appointed also the king’s portion of his substance for the burnt offerings, to wit, for the morning and evening burnt offerings, and the burnt offerings for the sabbaths, and for the new moons, and for the set feasts, as it is written in the law of the Lord. Moreover he commanded the people that dwelt in Jerusalem to give the portion of the priests and the Levites, that they might be encouraged in the law of the Lord.

schools.summary: Delitzsch adds the note of proportion, each man set according to the measure of his service, renders the disputed phrase as the camp of the Lord, identifies what the king gave as the material for the burnt offerings the law commands, and explains the purpose clause — the ministers were to be maintained so that they might hold to the law without being driven to work for their subsistence; Ellicott records the restoration of the Davidic rotation and renders the command plainly as the king speaking to the dwellers in Jerusalem.

Gill traces the courses to David, notes that they had run in Jehoshaphat's day and been interrupted since, and explains the king's gift as royal bounty beyond what kings usually supplied, the temple treasury being exhausted and the people left poor by the previous reign.

Clarke takes the tents of the Lord to mean the temple simply, that building being house and tabernacle and tent and camp at once, and reports the conjecture that the kings of Judah had furnished the daily sacrifice at their own charge since David's time.

Henry draws a rule from the arrangement, that good order contributes much to the carrying on of a good work, hears in the word tent a reminder that temple privileges are movable and this temple was shortly to be taken away, and states the principle of the king's gift — the people were liable, but rather than see them burdened he met the cost from his own estate.

debates.question: Why is the temple called the tents of the Lord?

positions.position: It means the temple with the court of the priests — the camp of the Lord.
It means the temple simply, that building being house, tabernacle, tent and camp of the Most High at once.
The word is pointed: temple privileges are movable things, and this temple was shortly to be removed.

themes: And Hezekiah appointed the courses of the priests and the Levites after their courses, every man according to his service, the priests and Levites for burnt offerings and for peace offerings, to minister, and to give thanks, and to praise in the gates of the tents of the Lord.

He appointed also the king’s portion of his substance for the burnt offerings, to wit, for the morning and evening burnt offerings, and the burnt offerings for the sabbaths, and for the new moons, and for the set feasts, as it is written in the law of the Lord.
Moreover he commanded the people that dwelt in Jerusalem to give the portion of the priests and the Levites, that they might be encouraged in the law of the Lord.

5.pericope_label: And as soon as the commandment came abroad, the children of Israel brought in abundance the firstfruits of corn, wine, and oil, and honey, and of all the increase of the field; and the tithe of all things brought they in abundantly. And concerning the children of Israel and Judah, that dwelt in the cities of Judah, they also brought in the tithe of oxen and sheep, and the tithe of holy things which were consecrated unto the Lord their God, and laid them by heaps. In the third month they began to lay the foundation of the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month.

schools.summary: Delitzsch divides the gifts, firstfruits to the priests and tithes to the whole tribe of Levi, insists the children of Israel here are emigrants from the north rather than its inhabitants, records without smoothing it that the law speaks of heave offerings from consecrated gifts rather than a tenth of them, and dates the heaps from the end of the grain harvest to the end of the fruit and wine harvest; Ellicott would strike the supplied word, places the third month at the close of wheat harvest, and marks the seventh as the month of Tabernacles, kept when the vintage was over.

Gill has the command carried beyond the capital into the cities of Judah, thinks the supplied word concerning can be dispensed with, identifies the third month as Sivan and puts it where barley harvest ended and wheat harvest began.

Clarke names the months from the Targum and explains what the heaps physically were, the vast collections of grain the tithes produced beyond what the givers consumed; Wesley takes the third month as the one in which their harvest began and the seventh as the one in which it ended.

debates.question: Where in the harvest does the third month fall?

positions.position: At the end of barley harvest and the beginning of wheat harvest.
At the close of wheat harvest.
At the beginning of the harvest season as a whole.

themes: And as soon as the commandment came abroad, the children of Israel brought in abundance the firstfruits of corn, wine, and oil, and honey, and of all the increase of the field; and the tithe of all things brought they in abundantly.

And concerning the children of Israel and Judah, that dwelt in the cities of Judah, they also brought in the tithe of oxen and sheep, and the tithe of holy things which were consecrated unto the Lord their God, and laid them by heaps.
In the third month they began to lay the foundation of the heaps, and finished them in the seventh month.

8.pericope_label: And when Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord, and his people Israel. Then Hezekiah questioned with the priests and the Levites concerning the heaps. And Azariah the chief priest of the house of Zadok answered him, and said, Since the people began to bring the offerings into the house of the Lord, we have had enough to eat, and have left plenty: for the Lord hath blessed his people; and that which is left is this great store.

schools.summary: Delitzsch records that the king and those with him blessed both the Lord and his people, insists the question was not whether the stores sufficed but how such masses had accumulated, thinks the identification with Uzziah's Azariah hardly possible on the arithmetic, and explains the infinitives absolute in the priest's reply as the grammar of animated speech; Ellicott leaves the identification open, renders the reply literally as eating and being satisfied and leaving over even unto abundance, and points out that what is called left over is what remained after the priests' own maintenance had been subtracted.

Gill identifies the heaps as tithes and firstfruits, allows that the king's question may have been why they had been left lying where they were, and gives Azariah's descent in the line of Zadok, passing on Jarchi's identification of him with the Azariah of Uzziah's reign.

debates.question: Is this Azariah the high priest who confronted Uzziah?

positions.position: Jarchi took him to be the same man.
Hardly, since that confrontation was some forty years earlier.
Possibly; if not, he is otherwise unknown.

themes: And when Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord, and his people Israel.
Then Hezekiah questioned with the priests and the Levites concerning the heaps.

And Azariah the chief priest of the house of Zadok answered him, and said, Since the people began to bring the offerings into the house of the Lord, we have had enough to eat, and have left plenty: for the Lord hath blessed his people; and that which is left is this great store.

11.pericope_label: Then Hezekiah commanded to prepare chambers in the house of the Lord; and they prepared them, And brought in the offerings and the tithes and the dedicated things faithfully: over which Cononiah the Levite was ruler, and Shimei his brother was the next. And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God.

schools.summary: Delitzsch sorts the hierarchy — Cononiah over the stores, his brother second, ten Levites beneath them, fourteen in all for the keeping, with separate officers for the distributing — identifies the Azariah named beside the king as the high priest who had answered him, and prefers to render the phrase of royal authority as by mandate; Ellicott confirms that the idiom means under Cononiah's orders, admits nothing is known of the ten beyond their names, and notes the unusual sense of the word for commandment, which ordinarily means a census.

Gill leaves open whether new chambers were built or existing ones fitted up, stresses the word faithfully — nothing kept back for private use — and describes the ten as assistants under the command of the first two, ready for whatever they were directed to do.

Henry treats the chambers and the officers as two halves of one trust: the stores were not to lie in loose heaps open to waste and embezzlement but to be locked up under treasurers, which he supports from the ant that provides her meat in summer and from the observation that the public gives cheerfully to what it sees well husbanded; and they were not to be hoarded longer than there was occasion, lest the rust become a witness against those who hoarded them.

themes: Then Hezekiah commanded to prepare chambers in the house of the Lord; and they prepared them,
And brought in the offerings and the tithes and the dedicated things faithfully: over which Cononiah the Levite was ruler, and Shimei his brother was the next.

And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God.

14.pericope_label: And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, the porter toward the east, was over the freewill offerings of God, to distribute the oblations of the Lord, and the most holy things. And next him were Eden, and Miniamin, and Jeshua, and Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah, in the cities of the priests, in their set office, to give to their brethren by courses, as well to the great as to the small: Beside their genealogy of males, from three years old and upward, even unto every one that entereth into the house of the Lord, his daily portion for their service in their charges according to their courses;

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott agree on Kore's charge of the freewill offerings and on the six Levites subordinate to him, and both place those six out in the priestly cities where they themselves were stationed rather than in Jerusalem; Delitzsch explains that the brethren they served included the Levites too young or too old to come up and those whose course was not on duty, and Ellicott would attach the phrase about their set office to the following verb, giving the sense honestly to give.

Gill identifies Kore as the porter at the east gate, takes his business to have lain chiefly with the priests in the temple and the capital, and gives Kimchi's reasons for the three-year threshold — a younger child could not come into the temple, had not the understanding to keep what was given him, and might defile an offering by handling it, while females were not admitted at any age.

Clarke records a manuscript variant in one of the six names, supported by the ancient versions; Wesley sums the office up without complication, as receiving the portions belonging to the priests and handing them on.

debates.question: Where did the six subordinate Levites distribute?

positions.position: Chiefly to the priests in the temple and in Jerusalem, under Kore.
In the priestly cities where they were themselves stationed.

themes: And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, the porter toward the east, was over the freewill offerings of God, to distribute the oblations of the Lord, and the most holy things.

And next him were Eden, and Miniamin, and Jeshua, and Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah, in the cities of the priests, in their set office, to give to their brethren by courses, as well to the great as to the small:

Beside their genealogy of males, from three years old and upward, even unto every one that entereth into the house of the Lord, his daily portion for their service in their charges according to their courses;

17.pericope_label: Both to the genealogy of the priests by the house of their fathers, and the Levites from twenty years old and upward, in their charges by their courses; And to the genealogy of all their little ones, their wives, and their sons, and their daughters, through all the congregation: for in their set office they sanctified themselves in holiness: Also of the sons of Aaron the priests, which were in the fields of the suburbs of their cities, in every several city, the men that were expressed by name, to give portions to all the males among the priests, and to all that were reckoned by genealogies among the Levites.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the parenthesis as prompted by the word register in the preceding line and would translate it in two halves, the priests enrolled by clans and the Levites from twenty upward standing in their offices by divisions; Delitzsch finds the following verse genuinely hard, rejecting one proposed supplement as arbitrary and another scholar's rendering of the key word while accepting his account of where the thread resumes, and settles the sense from the parallel construction in the verse after it; Ellicott adds that officers were appointed even for the priests and Levites living on farms beyond the sacerdotal cities.

Gill reads the parenthesis as recording that a portion was given to priests and Levites alike once they were entered in their family registers at the appointed age, and describes the suburb fields as the lands allowed the priests out of the several tribes, where they lived when their course was off duty and where a portion reached them as surely as it reached those in the capital.

themes: Both to the genealogy of the priests by the house of their fathers, and the Levites from twenty years old and upward, in their charges by their courses;
And to the genealogy of all their little ones, their wives, and their sons, and their daughters, through all the congregation: for in their set office they sanctified themselves in holiness:

Also of the sons of Aaron the priests, which were in the fields of the suburbs of their cities, in every several city, the men that were expressed by name, to give portions to all the males among the priests, and to all that were reckoned by genealogies among the Levites.

20.pericope_label: And thus did Hezekiah throughout all Judah, and wrought that which was good and right and truth before the Lord his God. And in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered.

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks the verse as the conclusion of the whole narrative and paraphrases its second half, that in every work begun for the service of the house of God and for the restoring of the law Hezekiah sought his God, did it with all his heart, and prospered; Ellicott glosses the third term of the verdict as faithfulness or sincerity, keeps the word for commandment singular as the Hebrew has it, reads the phrase about seeking God as in order to seek rather than as a condition, and sets the expression with all his heart beside the familiar language of a perfect heart.

Gill summarises the achievement — the courses settled and a provision made for the ministers and their households — and lists the works themselves: cleansing the temple, providing the sacrifices, placing the priests and Levites in order, taking care of their maintenance.

Clarke turns the three terms into a portrait of a worthy king — good and doing good, upright and maintaining justice, truly religious and living by the truth he has received as revelation — and ends with a wish, that God would always send such kings to the nations and that people blessed with them would be obedient and thankful.

themes: And thus did Hezekiah throughout all Judah, and wrought that which was good and right and truth before the Lord his God.
And in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law, and in the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered.
